Did the twentieth century refute postmillennialism?
Do the world wars and secularisation of the twentieth century, and postmillennialism's decline, count against it, and what does its later revival show?

Postmillennialism dominated much nineteenth-century American Protestantism, faded after the First World War, and revived from the 1970s among Reformed writers. Premillennialists often read the century as confirming biblical warnings of decline; postmillennialists distinguish their view from the liberal idea of progress; amillennialists warn against reading eschatology off the news.

Postmillennialists argue that their view's decline in the twentieth century reflected cultural mood and theological liberalism rather than exegetical refutation. Historian James Moorhead argues that among mainline Protestants after 1865 postmillennialism eroded into a general faith in progress and the Social Gospel, losing its supernatural content. Historic Reformed postmillennialism (Edwards, Hodge, Warfield) rested on texts such as the Great Commission and Psalm 110:1, and its revival through Rushdoony, Bahnsen, Gentry and Mathison, together with rapid church growth in Africa, Asia and Latin America, indicates in their view that it remains a live exegetical option.

Premillennial critics argue that the world wars, the Holocaust, totalitarian regimes and the secularisation of the historically Christian West were widely and reasonably taken as counting against postmillennial optimism. They see this as more than a change of mood: Scripture warns of worsening conditions, apostasy and a final tribulation (Matthew 24:21, 2 Thessalonians 2:3). Walvoord regarded postmillennialism as largely abandoned by mid-century, while premillennialism grew through Bible institutes and prophecy conferences, as historian Timothy Weber documents.

Postmillennialists answer that their eschatology is a claim about the long-term outcome of history, not any single century; Boettner and Gentry note that its timescale may be measured in millennia. They point to the growth of Christianity in sub-Saharan Africa and elsewhere from a small minority in 1900 to hundreds of millions today, and argue that attempts to match current events to prophecy have themselves produced many failed predictions.

Critics reply that if any setback can be absorbed by lengthening the timescale, the view becomes hard to test, and that Christianity's growth in the Global South has coincided with steep decline in former Christendom, which fits an expectation of mixed conditions better than progressive Christianisation. Many premillennialists also reject date-setting and 'newspaper exegesis' as abuses of their own view.

Amillennialists such as Hoekema and Riddlebarger argue that both postmillennial optimism and premillennial expectations of decline err when they treat history as a scorecard. The New Testament promises both gospel advance to all nations and tribulation throughout the age (Matthew 24:14, Acts 14:22), so neither world wars nor revivals measure the truth of an eschatology. The decline and revival of postmillennialism are sociological facts that settle nothing exegetically.

Postmillennialists agree that history is not the test of exegesis, which is their own point against the premillennial critique, but argue that amillennialism underweights texts promising that the nations will serve Christ before the end (Psalm 72:8-11, Isaiah 2:2-4, 1 Corinthians 15:25). These describe outcomes in history while sin and death still exist, which they say cannot be relocated to the new creation.

Amillennialists answer that these promises are fulfilled as the nations are gathered into the church now and are consummated when the kings of the earth bring their glory into the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:24-26). In their view the New Testament's use of these texts does not envision a golden age before the consummation.
Full preterism and the future resurrection
Were the Second Coming, resurrection and final judgment all fulfilled by AD 70, or does the creedal hope of a future bodily resurrection stand?

Full (consistent) preterism, or covenant eschatology, holds that all prophecy, including the parousia and resurrection, was fulfilled by AD 70. Partial preterists, amillennialists, postmillennialists and premillennialists reject this, and it stands outside historic creedal orthodoxy because the ecumenical creeds confess a future return and resurrection of the body; proponents reply that the creeds must be tested by Scripture.

Full preterists (covenant eschatology; Max King, Don Preston) argue that if the time texts are taken at face value, every prophesied end-time event, including the parousia, resurrection and judgment, must have occurred by AD 70. They read the resurrection of Daniel 12:2 and 1 Corinthians 15 as the corporate, covenantal raising of God's people from the death of the old covenant into new covenant life, completed when the temple fell; Daniel 12:7 ties these events to the shattering of 'the power of the holy people'. They see their view as consistent preterism, applying to all prophecy what partial preterists apply to some.

Partial preterists such as Mathison and Gentry argue the New Testament distinguishes AD 70 from a future, visible, bodily return: Jesus will come 'in the same way' as he was seen going (Acts 1:11); the body sown perishable is raised imperishable (1 Corinthians 15:42-44); and our mortal bodies will be given life and redeemed (Romans 8:11, 8:23). Paul condemned Hymenaeus and Philetus for saying 'the resurrection has already happened' (2 Timothy 2:17-18). Mathison's edited volume argues these texts cannot be reduced to a covenantal transition.

Full preterists respond that 'in the same way' in Acts 1:11 refers to the manner (in a cloud, then hidden from sight) rather than physical visibility to all, and that the 'body' (soma) of 1 Corinthians 15 is corporate, as in 'the body of Christ' (1 Corinthians 12:27). They read Hymenaeus' error as claiming the resurrection was already complete before its appointed time, which Paul could reject while still expecting it within that generation.

Critics answer that 1 Corinthians 15 is about individual bodies: the resurrection of 'the dead' is patterned on Christ's own bodily resurrection as firstfruits (15:20-23), and what is sown is the individual mortal body that must 'put on' immortality (15:42-44, 53). If the firstfruits was bodily, the harvest must be of the same kind. They also note that Paul gives no hint that Hymenaeus' error was merely premature.

Critics across the millennial positions note that the ecumenical creeds confess that Christ 'will come again' to judge the living and the dead, together with the resurrection of the body (Nicene Creed; Westminster Confession 32-33). Full preterism therefore stands outside historic creedal orthodoxy; Mathison and others regard it as a serious departure, since the church has never understood these articles as fulfilled in AD 70. They add that texts such as 1 Thessalonians 4:16 and John 5:28-29 describe a public event in which the dead leave their tombs.

Proponents respond that the creeds are subordinate standards to be tested by Scripture, a principle the Westminster Confession itself states (1.10), and that the Reformation also overturned long-standing consensus. They argue that creedal language of a future coming was formulated by largely Gentile churches that had lost sight of the Jewish covenantal context of AD 70, and ask to be answered exegetically rather than by appeal to tradition.

Critics reply that the Reformers revised doctrines they judged unbiblical but explicitly reaffirmed the ancient creeds' articles on Christ's return and the resurrection. They add that early post-apostolic writers, some writing after AD 70 (for example 1 Clement and the Didache), still expected a future coming and resurrection, which counts against the claim that the first audience understood these events as already fulfilled.
Daniel's seventieth week: a gap or continuous?
Is there a gap between the sixty-ninth and seventieth weeks of Daniel 9, placing the seventieth week in the future?

Dispensationalists see a gap of the church age between the sixty-ninth and seventieth weeks, with the seventieth week a future seven-year tribulation under the Antichrist. Partial preterists and postmillennialists read the weeks as continuous, fulfilled in Christ and the AD 70 judgment; many amillennialists, following Kline, read the seventy weeks symbolically, reaching to the consummation.

Dispensationalists (Walvoord, Pentecost, Hoehner) see a gap between the sixty-ninth and seventieth weeks of Daniel 9:24-27. The sixty-nine weeks (483 years) run from Artaxerxes' decree to the Messiah; Hoehner calculated 444 BC to AD 33 using 360-day prophetic years. Verse 26 places two events 'after' the sixty-two weeks (the Messiah cut off, and the city destroyed by 'the people of the prince who is to come') without placing them in the seventieth week. The 'he' who makes a firm covenant for one week (9:27) is that coming prince, the Antichrist, whose mid-week sacrilege matches the abomination of desolation Jesus placed in the future (Matthew 24:15, 2 Thessalonians 2:4).

Gentry and other preterists argue that the seventy weeks are a continuous 490-year unit: nothing in the text signals a gap, and inserting two thousand years into a number designed to measure time defeats the measurement. The 'he' of 9:27 most naturally refers to the Messiah, the main figure of 9:26, who confirms the covenant (compare 'the blood of the covenant', Matthew 26:28) and by his death in the middle of the week brings sacrifice to an end (Hebrews 10:8-18). The desolation of Jerusalem in AD 70 is the decreed consequence announced in 9:26-27.

Dispensationalists reply that the nearest antecedent of 'he' in 9:27 is 'the prince who is to come' (9:26), and that the verb (higbir) means to 'make strong' or enforce a covenant, suggesting a treaty rather than the new covenant. The six goals of 9:24, including 'to bring in everlasting righteousness' and 'to anoint a most holy place', have not been realised for Daniel's people and city, so the seventieth week must be future. Prophetic gaps occur elsewhere, as in Isaiah 61:1-2 read in Luke 4:18-21.

Postmillennial preterists answer that 'prince' in 9:26 stands in a dependent phrase ('the people of the prince'), so the subject of that clause is the people, and the Messiah remains the passage's central figure. They read the six goals of 9:24 (finishing transgression, atoning for iniquity, bringing everlasting righteousness) as accomplished in Christ's cross and the new covenant (Hebrews 9:26, Romans 3:21-26).

Kline and many amillennialists read the seventy weeks as a symbolic sabbatical period (seventy sevens, echoing the jubilee pattern of Leviticus 25 and the sabbath-years of 2 Chronicles 36:21) rather than a precise count of 490 years. The seventieth week begins with the Messiah's covenant-confirming work and extends symbolically through the church age to the consummation, with the desolator representing hostile powers until the decreed end. Riddlebarger argues this avoids both an arbitrary gap and the need to compress all fulfilment into the first century.

Dispensationalists reply that Daniel's prayer concerns Jeremiah's literal seventy years (Daniel 9:2, Jeremiah 25:11-12), so the answer of seventy 'sevens' naturally continues a literal reckoning. Hoehner's calculation landing on Jesus' final entry into Jerusalem suggests the sixty-nine weeks were exact, so the seventieth will be too. A symbolic week stretching across two thousand years, they argue, is a larger gap than the dispensational one.

Amillennialists answer that conservative calculations of the sixty-nine weeks vary widely depending on which decree and calendar are chosen, and that Hoehner's scheme relies on a 360-day year the text does not specify. Kline argues that Daniel 9, saturated with the vocabulary of the Mosaic covenant, points to theological rather than arithmetical precision.

Postmillennialism places Christ's return after the millennium, which most modern proponents (Gentry, Mathison, Bahnsen) identify with the whole period between the two advents: Christ already reigns from heaven, Satan is bound at the first coming, and the gospel progressively disciples the nations until the world is largely Christianized. An older Puritan and Edwardsean variant reserves the millennium for a future 'latter-day glory' near the end of the church age. Either way, there is one Second Coming, one general resurrection and one judgment at the close of history.
Cross and resurrection: decisive victory

Postmillennialists see the cross and resurrection as the definitive defeat of Satan and the enthronement of Christ, the ground for confidence that his kingdom will grow until it fills the earth (the stone of Daniel 2 that becomes a mountain).
Millennium: Christ's reign through the gospel

Mainstream modern postmillennialism (Gentry, Mathison) reads the 'thousand years' of Revelation 20 as a symbolic, lengthy era spanning the whole church age, marked by gradual, often uneven but real gospel growth. Older postmillennialists such as Jonathan Edwards and Charles Hodge placed a distinct golden age of the millennium in the latter part of this period, before Christ's return.
Satan bound so the nations can be reached

The binding of Revelation 20:3 is read as Christ's plundering of the 'strong man' at his first coming: Satan is restrained specifically from deceiving the nations, so that the Great Commission can succeed.
Pentecost: the kingdom's worldwide mission begins
The outpouring of the Spirit launches the discipling of the nations; Peter cites Psalm 110 to say Christ now reigns until his enemies are made his footstool.
Great Tribulation (AD 66–70)

Most contemporary postmillennialists are partial preterists and locate the Great Tribulation of the Olivet Discourse in the Jewish War, within 'this generation'. Historicist postmillennialists (many Puritans) instead spread tribulation imagery across church history.
Fall of Jerusalem
The destruction of the temple is read as Christ's judgment-coming on covenant-breaking Jerusalem, vindicating him and closing the old covenant era. It is not the Second Coming.
Large-scale conversion of the Jewish people

Many postmillennialists, following the Puritans (as surveyed by Iain Murray), expect a future mass conversion of ethnic Israel to Christ, bringing 'life from the dead' and a further flourishing of the gospel among the nations. Not all modern postmillennialists hold this.
Satan loosed: brief final rebellion
At the end of the long era of gospel success, Satan is released for a 'little season' and stirs a short-lived revolt (Gog and Magog), which is ended by Christ's appearing.
Second Coming

Christ returns once, visibly and bodily, to a largely Christianized world. Resurrection, judgment and the new creation follow as one complex of events; they are spaced out on this chart only for readability.
General resurrection
One resurrection of the righteous and the wicked together at the last day.
Final judgment
All people stand before Christ at the great white throne.
New heavens and new earth
The renewed creation is the final state. Some postmillennialists also see a present, covenantal 'new creation' begun in Christ (2 Corinthians 5:17), consummated here.

Amillennialism (a name many proponents find unhelpful; some prefer 'realized millennialism') holds that the thousand years of Revelation 20 is the present age between Christ's two comings: Satan is bound, departed believers reign with Christ in heaven, and the church lives in a tension of gospel advance and ongoing tribulation. The age ends with a brief intensification of evil, then one Second Coming, one general resurrection, one judgment and the new creation (Hoekema, Riddlebarger, Storms, following Augustine).
Cross, resurrection and ascension
Christ's death and exaltation inaugurate the 'already' of the kingdom; the last days have begun (Vos's two-age structure: the age to come has broken into this age).
Millennium: the present reign of Christ

The thousand years symbolize the complete era between the advents. The 'first resurrection' is either regeneration or (more commonly today) the souls of believers living and reigning with Christ in heaven during the intermediate state. Revelation 20 recapitulates the age rather than following chapter 19 chronologically.
Satan bound at the first advent
Satan is bound in a specific respect: he cannot prevent the gospel from going to the nations or gather them in a final assault before the appointed time.
Pentecost
The Spirit, the 'down payment' of the age to come, is given; the church is the one people of God from Jews and Gentiles.
Tribulation throughout the age

Amillennialists see tribulation as a mark of the whole church age (John is already 'in the tribulation'), with AD 70 as a terrible first-century instance and an intensification expected at the end. Views differ on how much of Matthew 24 refers to AD 70.

Many amillennialists read the first part of the Olivet Discourse as fulfilled in AD 70, which also serves as a type of the final judgment; some (e.g. Jay Adams) take a more thoroughly preterist reading of Revelation.
'All Israel' saved

Hoekema reads 'all Israel' in Romans 11:26 as the full number of elect Jews gathered throughout the age, shown here as a span. Others in the camp (Vos, Riddlebarger) expect a future large-scale turning of Jews to Christ before the end.
Satan loosed: apostasy and the man of lawlessness

Near the end, Satan is released for 'a little while'. Many amillennialists expect a final apostasy and a personal Antichrist (the man of lawlessness) who embodies the 'many antichrists' present in every age. Revelation 16:14, 19:19 and 20:8 are read as the same last battle.
One visible, bodily return of Christ ends the age. Resurrection, judgment and new creation follow as one event complex; they are spaced out on this chart only for readability.
Believers and unbelievers are raised together at 'the last day'.
One judgment of all people, the great white throne.
Amillennialists such as Hoekema stress that the eternal state is an earthly, renewed creation, where Old Testament land promises find their ultimate fulfilment.

Historic premillennialism (Ladd, Blomberg, Grudem, and in an early form Papias, Justin Martyr and Irenaeus) holds that the kingdom is inaugurated now but that Christ returns once, after a future Great Tribulation the church passes through, to raise believers and reign on earth for a millennium before the final resurrection and judgment. Unlike dispensationalism, it sees one people of God and no pre-tribulation rapture.
Cross and exaltation: the kingdom inaugurated
Ladd's 'already/not yet': the kingdom of God has come in Jesus' ministry, death and resurrection, but awaits consummation in stages.
The church, one people of God with Israel's believing remnant, begins its mission.
Church age: kingdom present, Satan active
Christ reigns from heaven and the kingdom advances, but Satan is not yet bound in the sense of Revelation 20 and evil persists until the end.
Ladd and Blomberg hold that the Olivet Discourse blends the near judgment on Jerusalem with the end of the age (prophetic foreshortening); AD 70 fulfils part of it and foreshadows the rest.
Future Great Tribulation and Antichrist
A final period of intense persecution under a personal Antichrist. The church is present and preserved through it rather than removed from it.
Second Coming (post-tribulational)

One glorious return 'after the tribulation of those days'. The 'rapture' is believers rising to meet the Lord in the air and escorting him back to earth, the sense Ladd gives to the Greek word apantēsis (a welcoming meeting).
First resurrection: believers raised

The 'first resurrection' of Revelation 20:4-5 is a bodily resurrection of the saints at Christ's coming. Ladd argues the same verb (ezēsan, 'came to life') must mean bodily life for both groups in verses 4 and 5.
Israel looks on the one they pierced
Many historic premillennialists expect a national turning of Jews to Christ at or near his return, joining the one people of God.
Millennium: Christ reigns on earth

Satan is bound and Christ reigns with his resurrected saints over a world in which mortal nations still live. Many treat 'a thousand years' as a long period rather than an exact count. Satan's binding begins here.
Satan loosed: Gog and Magog
At the end of the thousand years Satan deceives the nations once more and is finally defeated.
Second resurrection and final judgment
The 'rest of the dead' are raised and judged at the great white throne.
The eternal state follows the millennium.

Dispensational premillennialism (Darby, Scofield, Walvoord, Pentecost, Ryrie, Ice) distinguishes Israel and the church. The church age is a 'parenthesis' inserted before Daniel's seventieth week; Christ raptures the church before a future seven-year tribulation, returns visibly at its end, and reigns for a literal thousand years from Jerusalem, fulfilling God's unconditional promises to national Israel. Progressive dispensationalists (Blaising, Bock) see more continuity, but keep the same broad sequence.
Cross: Messiah 'cut off'
The sixty-nine weeks of Daniel 9 end with Messiah's rejection and death; the prophetic clock for Israel then pauses (the 'gap' before the seventieth week).
Pentecost: the church begins
The church, a distinct body formed by Spirit baptism and not foreseen in Old Testament prophecy (a 'mystery'), begins at Pentecost.
Fall of Jerusalem (not the Great Tribulation)

Luke 21:20-24 describes AD 70, after which Jerusalem is 'trampled' until the times of the Gentiles end. Matthew 24:15-31, by contrast, is read as still future; 'this generation' is taken as the generation that sees those signs.
Pre-tribulation rapture

Christ comes for his church, raising dead believers and catching up living ones, before the seventieth week begins. The church is promised deliverance from 'the wrath to come'. Midtribulation and prewrath variants place the rapture later in the week.
Seven-year tribulation (Daniel's 70th week)

Antichrist confirms a covenant with Israel, then breaks it at the midpoint by setting up the abomination of desolation in a rebuilt temple. The final three and a half years are the Great Tribulation, the 'time of Jacob's trouble' (Revelation 6–19).
Second Coming to earth
Christ returns with his saints, defeats the beast's armies at Armageddon, and judges the living nations.
National Israel saved and regathered
Surviving Israel turns to the Messiah and is regathered to the land, fulfilling the Abrahamic, Davidic and New covenant promises to the nation.
Old Testament saints and martyrs raised

Old Testament believers and tribulation martyrs are raised to share in the kingdom, completing the 'first resurrection', which dispensationalists see as occurring in phases (Christ, the church at the rapture, these saints).
Satan bound in the abyss
Satan is fully incapacitated for the thousand years; the binding is total, not partial.
Millennial kingdom

A literal thousand-year reign of Christ on David's throne in Jerusalem, with Israel at the head of the nations; many expect a millennial temple (Ezekiel 40–48). It ends with Satan's release and a final rebellion.
Great white throne judgment
The unbelieving dead are raised and judged (the second resurrection).
The eternal state; many dispensationalists hold that Israel and the church remain distinct even here, though progressive dispensationalists stress their unity.

Partial (orthodox) preterism holds that many prophecies, especially the Olivet Discourse's Great Tribulation and much of Revelation, were fulfilled in the first century, culminating in Christ's judgment-coming on Jerusalem in AD 70, while the bodily Second Coming, general resurrection and final judgment remain future. It is a hermeneutic combined with postmillennialism (Gentry, DeMar, Mathison) or amillennialism (Jay Adams); R. C. Sproul held it while leaving the millennial question more open. Much of its Revelation reading rests on a pre-70 date, which is disputed.
Seventy weeks fulfilled in Christ
Daniel's seventy weeks run continuously, with no gap, to Christ's ministry and death, which 'make an end of sins' and confirm the covenant; Jerusalem's destruction follows as the consequence.
Pentecost: the 'last days' of the old covenant
The 'last days' are the final generation of the old covenant order (AD 30–70), in which the gospel is preached to the known world before the end of that age.
The beast: Nero and Rome

Many partial preterists identify the beast of Revelation 13 with Nero (666 matching a Hebrew spelling of 'Nero Caesar') and his persecution of AD 64–68; Gentry links the man of lawlessness and the apostasy with the same era and the Jewish revolt. Some partial preterists still expect a future personal Antichrist.
The Jewish War, with Roman armies surrounding Jerusalem, is the tribulation Jesus said would fall on 'this generation'. Josephus's account is cited for its severity.
Christ's judgment-coming on Jerusalem

The 'coming on the clouds' of Matthew 24:30 and 26:64 is read, in Old Testament prophetic idiom (Isaiah 19:1), as Christ's vindication and enthronement displayed in judgment on the temple; the old covenant age ends. N. T. Wright reads the Olivet imagery similarly without adopting the label.
Kingdom age (millennium for postmillennial preterists)

After AD 70 the church carries on the mission of the established kingdom. Postmillennial preterists see the millennium of Revelation 20 here (they place its start at the first advent) and expect gospel success; amillennial preterists see the same period with more mixed expectations.
Millennium (inter-advent)

Most partial preterists read Revelation 20 as the present reign of Christ from the first advent to the second; whether it ends in near-universal gospel success (postmil) or not (amil) depends on the millennial view combined with this hermeneutic.
Future bodily Second Coming

Unlike full preterists, partial preterists insist on a future personal return. Many see a transition in the Olivet Discourse at Matthew 24:36 ('that day'), and read Acts 1:11 and 1 Corinthians 15 as still future.
Bodily resurrection
A future physical resurrection of all the dead, as confessed in the historic creeds.
Universal judgment at the end of history.
Consummated new creation
Some partial preterists read Revelation 21–22 as describing the new covenant order already begun after AD 70 (Gentry), while still expecting the final consummation of 2 Peter 3 and Romans 8.

Full preterism, which its proponents call 'covenant eschatology' (Max King, Don Preston), holds that all prophecy, including the Second Coming, the resurrection and the judgment, was fulfilled by AD 70, when the old covenant age ended. Believers now live in the new creation, which has no end. This places it outside the historic creeds (the Apostles' and Nicene creeds confess a future return and bodily resurrection), and critics including partial preterists (Gentry, Mathison) argue it misreads 1 Corinthians 15 and Acts 1:11. Proponents reply that the creeds are subordinate to Scripture and that the New Testament's time texts ('soon', 'this generation') must govern every eschatological promise.
Cross: covenant transition begins
Christ's death inaugurates the new covenant, but the old covenant world continues alongside it for a final generation.
Satan bound
Satan is bound by Christ's work; full preterists typically see him loosed for the 'little season' of the Jewish revolt and then destroyed by AD 70 (Romans 16:20: 'soon').
Millennium: the AD 30–70 transition

Most full preterists (following Max King) take the thousand years as symbolic of the forty-year transition between covenants; a minority place it elsewhere (for example, from AD 70 onward or in the pre-Christian period).
Pentecost: the 'last days' of the old age
The 'last days' are the closing years of the old covenant age, not of world history.
Antichrists and the beast
The 'many antichrists' were first-century apostates, and the beast and man of lawlessness are first-century figures (often Nero or a Jewish leader).
Shared with partial preterism: the Jewish War fulfils Matthew 24.
End of the age
The fall of the temple marks 'the end of the age' (Matthew 24:3): the old covenant world passes away, which proponents equate with 'heaven and earth' passing away.
The Parousia

Christ's one Second Coming happened in AD 70, in judgment and in the vindication of his people, as the time texts are said to require. Critics point to Acts 1:11 ('in the same way') and the lack of a visible, bodily return; proponents read 'in the same way' as a coming in clouds of glory.
Resurrection

Proponents most commonly take this as a corporate or covenantal resurrection: the people of God raised out of the 'death' of the old covenant into the life of the new (King's 'corporate body view'). Others hold an 'individual body at death' view, in which believers since AD 70 receive immortal bodies in heaven at death. Critics argue that 1 Corinthians 15 requires a future, physical resurrection.
Judgment
The judgment of the living and the dead is placed at AD 70. Many full preterists add that individuals are judged at death from then on.
New creation (covenantal), from AD 70 onward

The new heavens and new earth are the new covenant order, fully established in AD 70 and enduring without end. No future end of physical history is expected; the gospel goes on spreading. Proponents differ on whether the physical cosmos itself will ever change.

Historicism, the dominant Protestant reading from the Reformation to the nineteenth century (Luther, the Puritans, Isaac Newton, Albert Barnes, E. B. Elliott), reads Revelation and Daniel as a continuous prophetic chart of church history from the apostles to the end, usually applying the 'day-year principle' (1,260 days = 1,260 years) and identifying the papacy as Antichrist. The specific dates and identifications below follow common nineteenth-century schemes; proponents differed widely on details. Historicists were both postmillennial (most Puritans, Edwards) and premillennial (Elliott, Spurgeon); this chart follows the postmillennial pattern and notes the alternative.
